food.text: In the early Lunda Empire, settled farming and permanent villages were mostly limited to river valleys, since the land between rivers was harder to cultivate. Only the area just to the north of Lunda also allowed people to settle in these in-between spaces.

By the 17th century, Dutch and British immigrants introduced their own foodways to the Cape, adding to the existing culinary traditions of the Khoisan and Bantu communities there. This encounter began a long process of culinary blending between European and African foodways in the region.

Bantu peoples introduced agriculture to South Africa, cultivating grains, starchy fruits, and root tubers. Following the Columbian Exchange, crops such as maize, squash, and sweet potatoes arrived from the Americas and displaced the cultivation of many older Old World food crops.

Between 1700 and 1860, the Luba Empire expanded across Central Africa mainly by extracting tribute from smaller, densely populated states rather than conquering their land outright. This tribute system redistributed agricultural, hunting, and mining resources among the nobility, and the ruling class held a monopoly on trade goods such as salt, copper, and iron ore.

When Mutapa hunters killed an elephant, their families and friends joined them to cook and eat it at the site of the carcass. The population killed elephants by digging pits for them to fall into, or by spearing and incapacitating a sleeping elephant. Hunting was a popular sport that, besides its economic benefits, trained martial skills.

At the Cape, the Cape Malay community developed a distinctive cuisine drawing largely on Southeast Asian culinary traditions. The Dutch East India Company had brought enslaved people to the Cape from Bengal, Java and Malaysia, and the Cape Dutch style of cooking owes at least as much to their cookery as to the European styles imported by settlers. One signature dish, Cape Malay yellow rice, is a sweet preparation made with turmeric, raisins, cinnamon, and sugar.

From the late 1660s to about 1680, locusts, smallpox, measles and plagues devastated the Mutapa Empire, and the insecurity of the time made their effects worse. Many villages and fields were left abandoned, trade fell sharply, and Stan Mudenge estimated that over half of Mutapa's population may have died. Meanwhile the profit-seeking owners of land grants called prazos employed private armies that disrupted trade and regularly raided Mutapa vassals for cattle and slaves, and gold mining was largely abandoned out of fear.
French Huguenot refugees settled at the Cape, many of them establishing themselves in Franschhoek. They went on to play an instrumental role in developing South Africa's wine industry.

In 1735, Mwenemutapa João V allowed a bishop to reestablish several feiras, or trading markets, on the Zimbabwean Plateau in exchange for certain goods. The Portuguese traders who resettled these markets struggled to turn a profit and abandoned them after João V's death, amid the succession conflict that followed.

art.text: After 1700, King Misha mi-Shyaang a-Mbul of the Kuba Kingdom introduced wooden sculptures called ndop figures. Each was carved to resemble the king and to represent his individual reign.

The Capuchin missionary Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi da Montecuccolo published a long book in 1687 about Kongo. His illustrations, both in the unpublished Araldi manuscript in Modena and as engravings in the book, are important sources for daily life.
In 1506, the explorer Diogo de Alcáçova described the edifices of Great Zimbabwe in a letter to Manuel I of Portugal. He wrote that they were part of the larger kingdom of Ucalanga.

Vicente Pegado, captain of the Portuguese garrison of Sofala, first recorded the name Zimbabwe in 1531. He noted that the natives called the edifices Symbaoe, which in their language signifies 'court'.

In 1648 the visitor Giovanni Francesco da Roma described Mbanza Kongo's impressive two-story royal palace as the only such building in all of Kongo. The city also had some twelve churches, including São Salvador.
Every Kuba ndop figure included the king's ibol, a personal symbol. It worked much like a personal standard, marking whose reign the carving stood for.

The Portuguese traveler António Fernandes may have made the first European visit in 1513 to 1515. He reported fortified centers built of stone without mortar, though he made no reference to Great Zimbabwe itself.

By the early 17th century, Kongo oral tradition described the female spirit Nzambi as the one who gives mankind laws, ordinances, arts, games, and musical instruments. Music and the arts were thus placed among the gifts of the divine.

Portuguese traders heard about Great Zimbabwe in the early 16th century and linked it to gold production and long-distance trade. Two of their accounts mention an inscription above the entrance, written in characters unknown to the Arab merchants who had seen it.

After 1700, King Misha mi-Shyaang a-Mbul introduced wooden sculptures called ndop figures, carved to resemble the king and represent his individual reign. Each figure included the king's ibol, a personal symbol akin to a personal standard.

war.text: In 1510, at the Battle of Salt River, the Portuguese admiral Francisco de Almeida and sixty-four of his men were killed and his party was defeated by the Goringhaiqua, one of the Khoikhoi clans, using cattle that were specially trained to respond to whistles and shouts.

Firearms reached Kongo armies in stages. Portuguese musketeers were first added as a mercenary force, and by the 1580s a musketeer corps raised locally from resident Portuguese and their mixed-race Kongo children was a regular part of the main army in the capital.

The Angolan Wars were a long series of conflicts that lasted from 1579 to 1683 and drew in Portugal, Ndongo, Kongo, Matamba and the Dutch West India Company. Hostilities broke out when the king of Ndongo had the Portuguese merchant community in his capital massacred. He also massacred almost a thousand Kongolese who were there. Though few in number, the Portuguese fielded heavier equipment, but they depended even more on large numbers of African auxiliaries. Kongo and Ndongo both suffered severe demographic loss as a result of the conflict and civil war.

On 29 October 1665 Portuguese forces defeated the army of the Kingdom of Kongo at the Battle of Mbwila. King António I was killed in the final attempt to break the Portuguese formation, and the Portuguese decapitated him. More than 400 of Kongo's heavy infantry and many more archers died, along with the royal chaplain Francisco de São Salvador, and the king's seven-year-old son was captured. The king's head was buried by the Portuguese in a chapel on the Bay of Luanda, and Kongo's crown and sceptre were sent to Lisbon as trophies.

Queen Nzinga forged what is described as the largest coalition of Angolan states in the 17th century against the Portuguese. After Portugal restored its rule in 1648, she signed a peace in 1656 and shifted to a policy of subordination to Portugal and support for Catholicism.

At the Battle of Mbwila on October 29, 1665, King António I and many of the Kinlaza nobility were killed. António's head was taken to Luanda along with the captured boy heir, and the royal crown and sceptre were sent to Portugal as trophies. Robbed of king, heir and symbols of leadership, Kongo fell into a civil war between the houses of Kinlaza and Kimpanzu that lasted from 1665 to 1709. Entire populations were conscripted into the armies, and captives from both sides, along with their families and supporters, were enslaved. By the end the capital had been destroyed, and over thirty thousand were sold into Trans-Atlantic slavery after the defeat of the Antonians.

In the 18th century, the Luba Empire invaded the lands of the Songye people north of the Upemba Depression but did not conquer them outright. The campaign instead helped consolidate Luba power in the area while emphasizing the extraction of tribute over the seizure of territory.

Van Riebeeck's first Cape defence, Fort de Goede Hoop, was built of mud, clay and timber, with four corners or bastions. It was replaced by the Castle of Good Hope, built between 1666 and 1679, after he had left the Cape.

Ndongo built up its own musketeers from the 16th century. In 1585 its army deployed 40 musketeers against Portugal, and around 1648 the Ngola Nzinga fielded three Dutch artillery pieces in a failed siege of the Portuguese stronghold at Muxima.
The Dutch West India Company captured Benguela and Luanda in 1641 and allied with Queen Nzinga and the Kongo against the Portuguese. Salvador Correia de Sá restored Angola to Portuguese rule in 1648.

After a Portuguese army invaded southern Kongo in 1622 and defeated local forces at the Battle of Mbumbi, King Pedro II personally led a force that crushed the invasion at the Battle of Mbanda. Pedro II then wrote to the Dutch Estates General proposing an alliance to drive the Portuguese out of Angola.

In 1512 King Afonso I led a military campaign against the Kingdom of Ndongo. He wrote to King Manuel of Portugal that he had sent him 410 slaves captured in the war. By the 1510s, Portugal provided military help in exchange for a share of the people taken captive and enslaved in Kongo's wars of expansion. Slaves not sold to the Portuguese were kept as royal property or sold into Kongo's domestic slave market.

Firearms became familiar in Kongo over time. Sources on a 1781 battle say José's 30,000 soldiers were armed with musket and ball, and historian John Thornton says a Kongolese unit facing Portuguese forces in 1790 sometimes used artillery.

Three hundred and sixty musketeers served in the Kongo army against the Portuguese at the Battle of Mbwila. Provincial Kongo armies also had some musketeers, who served against a Portuguese invading army in 1622.

In 1647 the Dutch and their allies won the Battle of Kombi, but they could not dislodge the Portuguese from their forts. Kongo could send only small forces because King Garcia II was at odds with Daniel da Silva of Soyo. Reinforcements from Brazil in 1648 then forced the Dutch to withdraw.

In 1568 the invading Jagas drove Alvaro I from Mbanza Kongo and sacked the city. He reclaimed the capital with Portuguese military help, but had to yield Luanda to the Portuguese in payment. Luanda was the source of the nzimbu currency used in the kingdom.

Captain-major Luís Lopes de Sequeira won victories at Ambuíla in 1665, Ndongo in 1671, Libolo in 1679 and Katole in 1681, which decisively broke the resistance of the African kingdoms. At Ambuíla, King António of Kongo fell in combat leading an assault on the Portuguese gun-lines, and his severed head was buried at Luanda with great pomp. In Ndongo, the town of Pungo Andongo was stormed and the entire royal family captured. King João Hari, who tried to flee, was captured by a hostile lord, delivered to the Portuguese and beheaded. At Katole, Sequeira himself was assassinated by a Portuguese soldier. Conflict subsided greatly after the peace with Matamba in 1683.

In 1645 Garcia II tried to drive Daniel da Silva from Soyo but was defeated at the fortified position of Mfinda Ngula. His son and would-be heir, Afonso, was captured while leading the Kongo forces, and a campaign to free him in 1646 failed.

In 1680 Manuel de Nóbrega assassinated King Pedro III under a banner of truce, in revenge for the death of his brother, King Daniel I. Daniel had been killed in 1678 when Pedro marched on São Salvador with Jaga mercenaries and burnt most of the city to the ground. Nóbrega later ruled Mbamba Lovata for the Kimpanzu and used the power of Soyo to make war on all Kinlaza partisans within reach, including Queen Ana Afonso de Leão, the Kinlaza matriarch. The article says the partisans kept trying to kill each other even as the kingdom ceased to exist as a functioning state.

literature.text: Kongo was the earliest Bantu language to be written in Latin characters. The Portuguese also created a dictionary in Kongo, the first of any Bantu language.

Capuchin missionaries left very long accounts of Kongo, some of which are the best sources available today. Writers such as Girolamo Merolla da Sorrento (1688) and Antonio Zucchelli da Gradisca (1712) filled them with details of daily life, political events and religious observations.

Around 1648 a dictionary of Kongo was written for the use of Capuchin missionaries. It held some 10,000 words and was the first dictionary of any Bantu language. Kongo was also the earliest Bantu language to be written in Latin characters.

The Congo River was known as Zaire during the 16th and 17th centuries. Zaire comes from a Portuguese adaptation of the Kikongo nzadi o nzere, meaning river swallowing rivers. Congo gradually replaced it in English usage during the 18th century.

In 1624, the Portuguese Jesuit Mateus Cardoso edited and published a Kongo translation of the Portuguese catechism compiled by Marcos Jorge. Its preface says the translation was done by Kongo teachers from São Salvador. It was probably partly the work of Félix do Espírito Santo, who was also Kongo.

Around 1648, a dictionary of about 10,000 words was written for Capuchin missionaries. Its principal author was Manuel Robredo, a secular priest from Kongo who was named Francisco de São Salvador after he became a Capuchin.

Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi da Montecuccolo wrote a long book in 1687 that was often quoted, cited and translated. It became one of the fundamental sources for Central African history. His illustrations, in the unpublished Araldi manuscript in Modena and as engravings in his book, are important sources for daily life.

The Kongo dictionary's principal author was Manuel Robredo, a secular priest from Kongo. After he became a Capuchin he was named Francisco de São Salvador. The back of his dictionary also includes a two-page sermon written in Kongo.

The name Zimbabwe was first recorded in 1531 by Vicente Pegado, captain of the Portuguese garrison of Sofala. He noted that the natives called these edifices Symbaoe, which in their language signified court.
Diogo Gomes was born in 1557 in Kongo to Portuguese parents and became a Jesuit priest. A catechism was produced under his authority, but no version of it survives today.

João de Paiva was rector of the Jesuit college of São Salvador until 1642 and wrote an extensive chronicle of the country, which is now lost. Some of his material informed the Synopsis Annalium of António Franco, published in 1725.
Dutch visitors to Loango reported the word nkisi in their 1668 book Description of Africa. They wrote it as mokissie and used it for both a material item and the spiritual entity that inhabits it.

In the Kikongo catechism of 1624, the verb koma was used to translate "to crucify", to nail a person to a cross. The same root appears in koma nloka, meaning to hammer in a curse, which was the way people enlisted a nkondi's spirit to hunt down and harm someone with misfortune, accidents or sickness. The 1624 catechism probably reflects Christian language from a lost catechism of 1557.

When the Kikongo Catechism of 1624 needed a word for "holy", it used ukisi, a term for a substance with the characteristics of nkisi. The translators borrowed a word from Kongo spiritual thought to express a Christian idea.
An earlier Kongo catechism was produced under the authority of Diogo Gomes, a Jesuit priest born in 1557 in Kongo to Portuguese parents. No version of that catechism survives today.

science.text: Metal-working was a core craft of the Luba. The Luba people produced pottery, iron axes, bows and spears, and carvings partly clad in sheets of copper as routine goods.
Abraham Ortelius labelled Manicongo as the city at the mouth of the river in his world map of 1564. The name Congo comes from the Kingdom of Kongo, which lay on the river's southern bank.

Van Riebeeck came to the Cape with medical experience: he was the son of a surgeon, and after joining the Dutch East India Company in 1639 he served as an assistant surgeon in Batavia. He later argued for a refreshment station at the Cape of Good Hope after staying there 18 days.
Cape Town's Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden still has a few wild almond trees that survive from the early Cape settlement under Van Riebeeck.

politics.text: Afonso I ruled the Kingdom of Kongo from 1509 to 1542 or 1543. He centralized power in his capital at Mbanza Kongo, curtailed the power of the nobility, and expanded the kingdom's borders through war. Captives taken in those wars were enslaved and forcibly relocated to Mbanza Kongo, and he sent embassies to Lisbon and Rome.

The Angolan Wars were a long series of conflicts lasting from 1579 to 1683. They began when the king of Ndongo had the Portuguese merchant community in his capital massacred, and he also massacred almost a thousand Kongolese then at Kabasa. The conflicts drew in Portugal, the kingdoms of Ndongo, Kongo, Matamba, Kasanje and Libolo, and the Dutch West India Company. Kongo and Ndongo suffered severe demographic loss from the fighting and civil war, and Portugal ultimately emerged as the main power in the region.

Around 1625, an outsider named Shyaam a-Mbul a Ngoong usurped one of the local rulers and united the chiefdoms of the Kuba region under his leadership. Tradition says he had travelled to the Pende and Kongo kingdoms to learn from them. He then returned to build the Kuba Kingdom's political, social and economic foundations.

The Manyika kingdom in modern Zimbabwe and Mozambique was founded as a vassal of the Mutapa Empire around 1500. It gained independence in the early 17th century while Mutapa was embroiled in civil war. In the 1690s it was conquered by Changamire Dombo of the nascent Rozvi Empire.

Around 1625 Shyaam a-Mbul a Ngoong left the Kuba region to find enlightenment in the Pende and Kongo kingdoms. After learning all he could from them, he returned and built the Kuba political, social and economic foundations.

Dutch merchant Jan van Riebeeck landed at Table Bay in April 1652 with 82 men and 8 women to found a Dutch settlement. It was meant as a way station supplying fresh provisions to VOC fleets, because deaths on the voyage between the Dutch Republic and Batavia were very high. Of his original five ships, the Walvis and the Oliphant arrived late, having had 130 burials at sea. He was charged with building a fort, improving the natural anchorage, planting cereals, fruit and vegetables, and obtaining livestock from the indigenous Khoi people.

Afonso I of Kongo became king after his father died in 1506. His mother kept the death secret so he could reach the capital first, and he then won a brief civil war against his half brother Mpanzu a Kitima, who was killed in the fighting, either by falling into a punji trap during his army's rout or by being captured and executed. Before that Afonso had governed the province of Nsundi, and he was a fervent convert to Catholicism.

Queen Nzinga negotiated a peace treaty for Ndongo, then seized power and fought a civil war against the rival claimant Hari a Kiluanje, who sought Portuguese support. According to the article, she had her nephew and heir murdered after bribing his guardian to hand him over, and violently persecuted anyone who did not accept her authority. She sealed an alliance with the Imbangala by sacrificing an infant with a mortar and pestle, and she is credited with forging the largest coalition of Angolan states in the 17th century against the Portuguese. She signed a peace in 1656 and shifted to subordination to Portugal.

The Kuba Kingdom had an unwritten constitution, elected political offices, separation of political powers, and a judicial system with courts and juries. It also had a police force, a military and taxation. Its king, the nyim, was responsible to a court council in which all the Kuba subgroups were represented equally.

Toward the end of Afonso's life, his children and grandchildren maneuvered for the succession, and in 1540 plotters that included Portuguese residents made an unsuccessful attempt on his life. After he died, his son Pedro was overthrown in 1545 by Diogo, Afonso's grandson, and had to take refuge in a church. Descendants of three of Afonso's daughters provided many later kings.

After the Mwene Muji polity lost its unity in the early 17th century, successor kingdoms broke away, including the Boma Kingdom, Yaka Kingdom and Bozanga. The first written record of Mwene Muji came in 1591 from the Italian explorer Filippo Pigafetta. He placed it in East Africa on his map.

philosophy.text: In 1704, after an illness, a young Kongo noblewoman named Dona Beatriz began to preach that she was possessed by Saint Anthony of Padua. Her movement, called Antonianism, blended Catholicism with Kongo religious rituals and nativism. It formed between 1704 and 1708.

King Afonso I of Kongo tried to make his kingdom a Catholic country by establishing the church, financing it from tax revenues and creating schools. He also sought to develop an appropriate theology that would merge Kongo's own religious traditions with Christianity.

The Bakongo cosmos is split between two worlds: the physical world, ku nseke, and the spiritual world, ku mpèmba. Ancestor veneration is described as the core principle of Kongo spirituality, and expert healers called Banganga train to commune with the ancestors.

Dona Beatriz was trained as an nganga marinda, someone who consults the supernatural world to solve community problems. She acted as a medium for Saint Anthony's pronouncements. Her teachings placed Jesus's birth in Mbanza Kongo and his baptism in the northern province of Nsundi.

Bakongo cosmology follows the Sun's rising, peaking, setting and absence, which match four stages of life: conception, birth, maturity and death. Everything transitions through these stages, even ideas. The cycle is drawn as a circle with a cross inside, called the Yowa or dikenga cosmogram.

In the 17th century, the Bakongo expanded the concept of nkisi to include consecrated objects or charms holding the essence of nature spirits and their spiritual powers. These minkisi were used for protection and healing.

By 1516 there were over 1000 students in the royal school Afonso founded, and schools in the provinces eventually produced a fully literate noble class. Afonso sent children and nobles to Europe to study. His son Henrique Kinu a Mvemba was elevated to bishop in 1518.

Dona Beatriz prophesied a new golden age that would follow the end of European presence in Kongo, with trees turning to silver and gold. She acknowledged papal authority but taught that European missionaries were corrupt and unsympathetic to the spiritual needs of Kongolese Catholics.

Dona Beatriz sent missionaries to urge the rulers of the divided Kongo territories to unite under one king, hoping to end the civil wars. In 1706, Pedro IV had her arrested and burned at the stake for heresy, under the urging of Portuguese Capuchin monks.

In 1624, the Portuguese Jesuit Mateus Cardoso published a Kongo translation of a Portuguese catechism compiled by Marcos Jorge. The preface says Kongo teachers from São Salvador did the translation. Kongo was the earliest Bantu language written in Latin characters.

Nkondi are aggressive minkisi, whose spirit was meant to travel out, hunt down and harm wrong-doers, witches or enemies. A frequently used expression for hammering nails into one is koma nloka, meaning to attach or hammer in a curse, a curse that could bring misfortune, accidents or sickness on its target. In the 1624 catechism, the verb koma was used to translate 'to crucify'. Some scholars think Portuguese missionaries brought images of Christ nailed to the cross and of the martyr Saint Sebastian, and that this iconography may have influenced the tradition, though Wyatt MacGaffey argues against it.

culture.text: Afonso I, who reigned over Kongo from 1509 to 1542 or 1543, worked hard to make Kongo a Catholic country. He set up the Roman Catholic Church, paid for it from tax revenues, and created schools. By 1516 there were over 1000 students in the royal school.

In 1704 a young Kongo noblewoman named Dona Beatriz began to preach that she was possessed by St. Anthony of Padua. Her Antonian movement mixed Kongo religious rituals with Catholicism, and she became known for healing and other miracles. In 1706 King Pedro IV had her burned at the stake for heresy.

The red powder tukula, made from ground cam wood, was central to Kuba ideas of beauty. It decorated the face, hair and chest during dances and important ceremonies, and it was used to anoint bodies for burial. It was also mixed with other pigments to dye raffia cloth.

King Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptized on 3 May 1491 and took the name João. He abandoned the new faith in 1495, partly because the Church required monogamy. He could not give up polygamy, since power in Kongo was elective and followed a matrilineal structure.

In 1663 the Hungarian Capuchin priest Padre Berdardino d'Ungheria baptized the king of Loango as Afonso, along with 6,000 of his subjects. When the king died there was a civil war, and the Christian party was defeated in 1665.

Capuchin missionaries left very long accounts of Kongo, full of details of daily life, political events and religious observations. Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi da Montecuccolo's long book of 1687 became one of the fundamental sources for Central African history. His illustrations are important sources for daily life.

Afonso I sought a theology that could merge Kongo's own religious traditions with Christianity. He studied theological textbooks, reportedly falling asleep over them, according to the Portuguese royal chaplain Rui de Aguiar. He also sent many of his children and nobles to Europe to study, including his son Henrique Kinu a Mvemba, who became a bishop in 1518.

Kuba boxes, called ngedi mu ntey by the Kuba, were generally used to hold tukula powder and paste. They could be square with a faceted lid, semicircular, rectangular, or shaped like a mask. Sometimes they held razors for cutting raffia, hairpins, or ritual objects.

In 1625 the Jesuits opened the college of São Salvador in Kongo. It was responsible for the education of most of the Kongo elite in the mid 17th century. Its rector until 1642, João de Paiva, also wrote an extensive chronicle of the country, now lost.

Antonian artifacts survive as St. Anthony figurines made of ivory, brass and wood. Called Toni Malau, or "Anthony of good fortune", they were fixed to crosses, used as staff finials, and worn as pendants. They were meant to guard their bearers against illness and other misfortunes.
